zh: 第二、明懺悔方法，即為三意：一、正明懺悔法不同；二、明罪滅階降；三、明復不復相。第一、正明懺悔法不同者，滅罪之由，各有其法，如衣垢膩，若直以水浣，終不可脫，皂莢灰汁，則能去之。滅罪之法亦復如是。今明懺悔方法，教門乃復眾多，取要論之，不過三種：一、作法懺悔，此扶戒律，以明懺悔；二、觀相懺悔，此扶定法，以明懺悔；三、觀無生懺悔，此扶慧法，以明懺悔。此三種懺悔法，義通三藏摩訶衍，但從多為說：前一法多，是小乘懺悔法；後二法多，是大乘懺悔法。
en: Second, clarifying the method of repentance: this has three parts — first, rightly clarifying that the methods of repentance differ; second, clarifying the different grades by which offenses are extinguished; third, clarifying whether restoration is complete or not.

First, rightly clarifying that the methods of repentance differ: the means by which an offense is extinguished each has its own particular method — just as cloth stained with grime cannot be freed of the stain by plain water alone, but soap-pod ash-lye is able to remove it. The methods for extinguishing an offense are exactly the same. Here, in clarifying the methods of repentance, the gates of teaching are indeed numerous, but taking the essentials, they number no more than three: first, repentance through formal procedure, which supports and clarifies repentance by means of the moral precepts; second, repentance through the contemplation of signs, which supports and clarifies repentance by means of concentration; third, repentance through the contemplation of no-arising, which supports and clarifies repentance by means of wisdom. These three methods of repentance, in their meaning, extend across both the Tripiṭaka and the Mahāyāna alike — but, speaking in terms of which predominates: the first method is, for the most part, the Hīnayāna's own method of repentance; the latter two are, for the most part, the Mahāyāna's own methods.

zh: 初明作法懺悔者，以作善事反惡事故，故名懺悔。如《毘尼》中，一向用此法滅罪。何以故？如懺第二篇：「二十眾作別住、下意、出罪等羯磨作法成就，即名為滅。」此不論見種種相貌，亦不論智慧觀空，故知但是作法懺悔。羯磨，此翻作法，如是乃至下三篇，並是作法。此事易知，義如律中廣明。但未明懺悔四重法，別有《最妙初教經》出懺悔四重法。彼經云：「當請三十清淨比丘僧，於大眾中，犯罪比丘當自發露。僧為作羯磨成就，又於三寶前作諸行法，及誦戒千遍，即得清淨。」亦云：「令取得相為證，而說罪滅清淨。」當知律中雖不出，經中有此羯磨明文，作法相貌如彼經中廣說。
en: First, clarifying repentance through formal procedure: because a wholesome act is undertaken to turn back an unwholesome one, this is called repentance. As in the Vinaya, this method alone is used to extinguish offenses. Why is this? As in repenting a second-category offense: "Once the assembly of twenty carries out to completion the formal procedures of probation, humbling of the mind, and release from the offense, this is called extinguished." This makes no mention of seeing various signs, nor of wisdom's contemplation of emptiness — hence it is known that this is repentance through formal procedure alone. "Karman," rendered here as "formal procedure," applies in the same way all the way down to the lower three categories of offense — all are matters of formal procedure. This matter is easily understood, and its meaning is explained in full in the Vinaya.

As for the method of repentance for the four grave offenses, which the Vinaya itself does not set out — there is a separate work, the Sūtra of the Most Sublime Initial Teaching, which gives the method of repenting the four grave offenses. That sūtra states: "One should invite thirty pure bhikṣus; before the great assembly, the offending bhikṣu should openly disclose the offense. Once the assembly carries out the formal procedure to completion, and further, before the Three Jewels, carries out the various practices and recites the precepts a thousand times, purity is thereby attained." It also states: "Let a sign be obtained as confirmation, and let the extinguishing and purification of the offense then be declared." One should know, then, that although the Vinaya itself does not set this out, the sūtras do contain this explicit statement of a formal procedure — the manner of carrying it out is explained fully in that sūtra.

The three methods track the three preliminary conditions the treatise keeps circling back to — precepts, concentration, wisdom — and each supports a progressively deeper kind of purification. Formal-procedure repentance is closest to what a Western reader might expect from "confession": a defined communal ritual with a clear beginning and end. For the lighter categories the ritual's correct performance suffices; but for the four grave offenses, the Sūtra of the Most Sublime Initial Teaching adds that a sign must be obtained as confirmation before the offense is declared extinguished.

items.en: Repentance through the Contemplation of Signs

zh: 二、明觀相懺悔者，行人依諸經中懺悔方法，專心用意，於靜心中見種種諸相，如菩薩戒中所說。若懺十重，要須見好相乃滅相者，佛來摩頂，見光、華種種瑞相已，罪即得滅。若不見相，雖懺無益。諸大乘方等陀羅尼行法中，多有此觀相懺法。三藏及《雜阿含》中亦說觀相懺悔方法，謂作地獄、毒蛇、白毫等觀相成就，即說罪滅。此悉就定心中作故，觀相懺悔多依修定法說。
en: Second, clarifying repentance through the contemplation of signs: the practitioner, following the methods of repentance found across the various sūtras, applies the mind single-mindedly and, within a stilled mind, sees various signs, as described in the bodhisattva precepts. If one is repenting the ten major precepts, a favorable sign must be seen before the offense can be said to be extinguished — the Buddha coming to rub the crown of one's head, or seeing light, flowers, and other auspicious signs — once such a sign is seen, the offense is thereupon extinguished; if no sign is seen, then even repentance brings no benefit. Among the various Mahāyāna Vaipulya dhāraṇī practice-methods, this kind of sign-contemplation repentance is found extensively. The Tripiṭaka and the Saṃyukta Āgama likewise speak of the method of sign-contemplation repentance — describing, for instance, the contemplation of hell, of poisonous snakes, or of the white curl of hair between the Buddha's brows, brought to completion, at which point the offense is declared extinguished. All of this is carried out within a concentrated mind, and so sign-contemplation repentance is, for the most part, explained in terms of the cultivation of concentration.

zh: 問曰：見種種相，云何知罪滅？答曰：經說不同，罪法輕重有異，不可定判。今但舉要而明，相不出四種：一、夢中見相；二、於行道時聞空中聲，或見異相及諸靈瑞；三、坐中覩見善、惡、破戒、持戒等相；四、以內證種種法門道心開發等為相。此隨輕重判之，不可定說，在下至驗善惡根性，更當略出。問曰：魔羅亦能作此等相，云何可別？答曰：實爾，邪正難別，不可定取。若相現時，良師乃識，事須面決，非可文載，是故行者初懺悔時，必須近善知識，別邪正之人。復次，夫見相者，忽然而覩，尚邪正難知，若逐文作心求之，多著魔也。問曰：若爾者，不應名觀相懺悔。答曰：言觀相者，但用心行道，功成相現，取此判之，便知罪滅、不滅。非謂行道之時，心存相事，而生取著。若如此用心，必定多來魔事。問曰：觀相懺悔行法云何？答曰：方法出在諸大乘方等修多羅中，行者當自尋經，依文而行。
en: Question: When these various signs are seen, how does one know that the offense is truly extinguished? Answer: The sūtras do not speak with one voice on this, since offenses differ in gravity, and no single fixed judgment can be given. Here, taking only the essentials, the signs do not exceed four kinds: first, seeing a sign in a dream; second, hearing a voice from empty space while walking the path, or seeing an extraordinary sign or other numinous, auspicious mark; third, beholding, while sitting, a sign of good, of evil, of having broken the precepts, or of having upheld them; fourth, taking as a sign the opening up of the mind of the path through various inwardly realized dharma-gates. These are judged according to gravity, and no fixed statement can be given — this will be given in brief again further below, where the marks that verify wholesome and unwholesome capacity are examined.

Question: Māra, too, is able to produce signs of this kind — how, then, can they be distinguished? Answer: This is indeed so; the deviant and the correct are hard to distinguish, and no fixed rule can be given. When such a sign appears, only a good teacher can properly recognize it — this is a matter that must be settled face to face, and cannot be conveyed through writing alone. This is why a practitioner, when first taking up repentance, must draw near to a good spiritual friend, someone able to distinguish the deviant from the correct. Furthermore, as for seeing a sign at all: it is beheld quite suddenly, and even then the deviant and the correct are hard to know — if one chases after the written description and forces the mind to seek such a sign out deliberately, one will, in most cases, fall prey to demonic interference.

Question: If this is so, then this should not be called repentance through the contemplation of signs at all. Answer: What is meant by "contemplation of signs" is only this: applying the mind to walking the path, and, once this effort bears fruit, a sign appears of itself — one then takes this sign as a basis for judgment, and so comes to know whether the offense is extinguished or not. It does not mean that, while walking the path, the mind should dwell on the matter of a sign and give rise to grasping after it. If the mind is used in that way, demonic interference is certain to follow in abundance. Question: What is the actual method of practice for repentance through the contemplation of signs? Answer: The method is set out across the various Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras; the practitioner should seek out these sūtras directly and practice in accordance with their text.

This is a notably cautious, almost clinical treatment of visionary experience for a meditation manual: signs of purification are real and expected, but the same signs can be produced by demonic interference, and the text is explicit that "the deviant and the correct are hard to distinguish" even for the practitioner having the experience — hence the repeated insistence on finding a qualified teacher rather than relying on textual checklists alone. The warning against "chasing after the written description" is aimed squarely at readers of exactly this kind of text: naming the four categories of sign is meant to orient understanding, not to hand a practitioner a target to manufacture.

items.en: Repentance through the Contemplation of No-Arising

zh:
三、明觀無生懺悔者，如《普賢觀經》中偈說：
一切業障海，皆由妄想生，
若欲懺悔者，端坐念實相。
眾罪如霜露，慧日能消除，
是故至誠心，懺悔六情根。
夫行人欲行大懺悔者，應當起大悲心，憐愍一切，深達罪源。所以者何？一切諸法本來空寂，尚無有福，況復罪耶？但眾生不善思惟，妄執有為而起無明及與愛恚，從此三毒廣作無量無邊一切重罪，皆從一念不了心生。
en:
Third, clarifying repentance through the contemplation of no-arising: as the Samantabhadra Contemplation Sūtra says in verse:
"The whole ocean of every karmic obstruction arises entirely from deluded thought;
If one wishes to repent of it, sit upright and be mindful of true reality.
Every offense is like frost or dew, which the sun of wisdom can dissolve away;
Hence, with a mind of utmost sincerity, repent at the very root of the six faculties of feeling."
A practitioner wishing to carry out this great repentance should give rise to a mind of great compassion, feeling for all beings, and penetrate deeply to the very source of offense. Why is this? All dharmas whatsoever are, from the very beginning, empty and still — there is not even merit to be found there, how much less offense? It is only that sentient beings, failing to reflect rightly, wrongly cling to conditioned existence and thereby give rise to ignorance, along with craving and aversion; and from these three poisons, every measureless and boundless grave offense is committed at length — all of it arising from a single thought-moment of unenlightened mind.

zh: 若欲除滅，但當反觀如此心者從何處起？若在過去，過去已滅，已滅之法則無所有，無所有法不名為心；若在未來，未來未至，未至之法即是不有，不有之法亦無此心；若在現在，現在之中，剎那不住，無住相中，心不可得。復次，若言現在，現在者，為在內、外、兩中間耶？若言在內，則不待外，內自有故；若言在外，於我無過。復次，外塵無知，豈得有心？既無內、外，豈有中間？若無中間，則無停處。如是觀之，不見相貌，不在方所，當知此心畢竟空寂。既不見心，不見非心，尚無所觀，況有能觀？無能無所，顛倒想斷。既顛倒斷，則無無明及以愛恚。無此三毒，罪從何生？
en: If one wishes to remove and extinguish this, one need only turn contemplation back and ask: from where does this mind arise? If it is in the past, the past has already ceased, and a dharma already ceased possesses nothing at all — and what possesses nothing at all cannot be called mind. If it is in the future, the future has not yet arrived, and what has not yet arrived simply does not exist — and what does not exist likewise has no mind in it. If it is in the present, then within the present itself, not a single moment remains still — and within a mark that never remains still, mind cannot be found.

Furthermore, if it is said to be in the present, is the present located inside, outside, or in between the two? If it is said to be inside, then it does not depend on the outside, since it would already exist within of itself; if it is said to be outside, then it has nothing to do with me. Furthermore, an external object has no awareness of its own — how, then, could it possess mind? Since there is neither inside nor outside, how could there be any "in between" at all? And if there is no "in between," there is nowhere for it to come to rest.

Contemplated in this way, no mark or appearance is seen anywhere, in any location whatsoever — one should know, then, that this mind is, in the end, empty and still. Since mind itself cannot be found, nor can "not-mind" be found either — there is not even anything to be contemplated at all, how much less anyone who contemplates? With neither a contemplating subject nor a contemplated object, every inverted thought is cut off. And once inverted thought is cut off, there is no more ignorance, nor craving and aversion. Without these three poisons, from where could offense possibly arise?

zh: 復次，一切萬法，悉屬於心，心性尚空，何況萬法？若無萬法，誰是罪業？若不得罪，不得不罪，觀罪無生，破一切罪，以一切諸罪根本性空，常清淨故。故維摩羅詰謂優波離：「彼自無罪，勿增其過，當直爾除滅，勿擾其心。」又如《普賢觀經》中說：「觀心無心，法不住法，我心自空，罪福無主，一切諸法皆悉如是，無住無壞。作是懺悔，名大懺悔，名莊嚴懺悔，名破壞心識懺悔，名無罪相懺悔。行此悔者，心如流水，念念之中見普賢菩薩及十方佛。」故知深觀無生，名大懺悔，於懺悔中最尊最妙。一切大乘經中明懺悔法，悉以此觀為主。若離此觀，則不得名大方等懺也。
en: Furthermore: the ten thousand dharmas all belong to mind — and if the very nature of mind is empty, how much more so the ten thousand dharmas? If there are no ten thousand dharmas, who is it that commits karmic offense? If offense cannot be found, then non-offense cannot be found either — contemplating offense as unarisen dissolves every offense whatsoever, since the very root-nature of every offense is empty, and ever pure.

Hence Vimalakīrti said to Upāli: "They are, of themselves, without offense — do not add to their fault. It should simply be removed and extinguished directly; do not disturb their minds." And likewise the Samantabhadra Contemplation Sūtra says: "Contemplating mind, no mind is found; dharmas do not abide in dharmas; my own mind is, of itself, empty, and offense and merit have no master over them — every dharma whatsoever is exactly the same, neither abiding nor perishing. Repentance carried out in this way is called great repentance, called adorned repentance, called the repentance that breaks apart mind and consciousness, called the repentance in which no mark of offense remains. One who practices this repentance has a mind like flowing water, beholding the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra and the buddhas of the ten directions in every single thought-moment." Hence it is known that the deep contemplation of no-arising is called great repentance — the most honored, the most sublime of every form of repentance. In every Mahāyāna sūtra that explains the method of repentance, this contemplation is taken as the essential core. Apart from this contemplation, none can rightly be called the great Vaipulya repentance.

zh: 問曰：觀無生懺悔，云何知罪滅相？答曰：如是用心，於念念中即諸罪業念念自滅。若欲知障道法轉者，精勤不已，諸相亦當自現，觀此可知。如前觀相中所說，善夢靈瑞、定慧開發等相，此中應具明。復次，若行者觀心與理相應，即是罪滅之相，不勞餘求，故《普賢觀經》中言：「令此空慧與心相應，當知於一念中能滅百萬億阿僧祇劫生死重罪。」以此為證，若得無生忍慧，則便究盡罪源，此則尸羅清淨，可修禪定。
en: Question: In repentance through the contemplation of no-arising, how does one know the mark of the offense's extinguishing? Answer: Using the mind in this way, every karmic offense is, moment by moment, extinguished of itself, moment by moment. If one wishes to know that the dharmas obstructing the path are being transformed, then, through unceasing diligence, the various signs will also naturally appear of themselves — by observing these, it can be known. As already stated above in the discussion of sign-contemplation — favorable dreams, numinous and auspicious marks, the opening of concentration and wisdom, and the like — the same signs should be understood to apply fully here as well.

Furthermore, if a practitioner's contemplating mind comes into accord with principle itself, this is precisely the mark of the offense's extinguishing, with no further confirmation needed elsewhere. Hence the Samantabhadra Contemplation Sūtra says: "Let this wisdom of emptiness come into accord with the mind, and know that, within a single thought-moment, it is able to extinguish the grave offenses of birth-and-death accumulated across a million koṭis of incalculable eons." Taking this as confirmation: if the wisdom of the forbearance of no-arising is attained, then the very source of offense is thereby exhausted to its root — and this is precisely when moral discipline becomes pure, and dhyāna-concentration may be cultivated.

This is the treatise's second sustained excursion into explicit emptiness-analysis, and it runs a close parallel to fascicle 1's tetralemma against "contaminated dharma": here the target is offense itself, sought and never found across past, future, present, inside, outside, and in between. The Vimalakīrti citation is worth pausing on — Upāli was the Buddha's own foremost expert in monastic discipline, and the scene invoked (from the Vimalakīrti Sūtra) has the layman Vimalakīrti correcting the Vinaya specialist on the deepest nature of an offense he was trying to help a guilt-stricken monk resolve through ordinary procedure. Note carefully what this section does not claim: it never says moral discipline stops mattering once emptiness is realized — the very next section still treats formal-procedure and sign-contemplation repentance as real and necessary for those who need them. Emptiness completes the picture; it does not replace conduct.

quiz.q: The methods of repentance number no more than three. What does each support?
options: procedure: concentration; signs: wisdom; no-arising: precepts
all three support wisdom
formal procedure supports precepts; contemplation of signs supports concentration; contemplation of no-arising supports wisdom
all three support precepts
quiz.why: "First, repentance through formal procedure, which supports and clarifies repentance by means of the moral precepts; second, repentance through the contemplation of signs ... by means of concentration; third, repentance through the contemplation of no-arising ... by means of wisdom."

quiz.q: Broadly, how are the three methods divided between the Hīnayāna and Mahāyāna?
options: all three are Mahāyāna only
all three are Hīnayāna only
in meaning they span both, but for the most part the first is Hīnayāna and the latter two Mahāyāna
the first two Hīnayāna, the last Mahāyāna
quiz.why: "These three methods of repentance, in their meaning, extend across both the Tripiṭaka and the Mahāyāna alike — but ... the first method is, for the most part, the Hīnayāna's own method of repentance; the latter two are, for the most part, the Mahāyāna's own methods."

quiz.q: What simile shows that each offense has its own method of extinction?
options: grimy cloth that plain water cannot clean but soap-pod lye can
carrying a bowl of oil
a debt paid to the strongest creditor
a cold-illness patient taking ginger and cinnamon
quiz.why: "The means by which an offense is extinguished each has its own particular method — just as cloth stained with grime cannot be freed of the stain by plain water alone, but soap-pod ash-lye is able to remove it." Ginger and cinnamon belong to the discussion of restoration.

quiz.q: Why does the Vinaya's procedure for second-category offenses show it is formal-procedure repentance only?
options: because a favorable sign must be seen
because one must contemplate mind as unarisen
because the precepts must be recited a thousand times
once the assembly of twenty completes the procedures it is called extinguished, with no mention of signs or contemplating emptiness
quiz.why: "Once the assembly of twenty carries out to completion the formal procedures ... this is called extinguished. This makes no mention of seeing various signs, nor of wisdom's contemplation of emptiness — hence it is known that this is repentance through formal procedure alone." Reciting the precepts a thousand times belongs to the four grave offenses.

quiz.q: The Vinaya gives no method for repenting the four grave offenses. Which sūtra does the text rely on, and what is the procedure?
options: the Sublime Supreme Concentration Sūtra: sit with a straightforward mind

the Sūtra of the Most Sublime Initial Teaching: invite thirty pure monks, disclose before the assembly, the saṅgha performs the procedure, practices before the Three Jewels, recite the precepts a thousand times
the Samantabhadra Contemplation Sūtra: sit upright mindful of reality
the Yingluo Sūtra: the four vows
quiz.why: "There is a separate work, the Sūtra of the Most Sublime Initial Teaching, which gives the method of repenting the four grave offenses. That sūtra states: 'One should invite thirty pure bhikṣus; before the great assembly, the offending bhikṣu should openly disclose the offense ... and recites the precepts a thousand times, purity is thereby attained.'"

quiz.q: According to the bodhisattva precepts, what must happen for the ten major offenses to be extinguished through repentance?
options: no sign needed, sincerity suffices
a favorable sign must be seen, such as the Buddha rubbing one's crown or light and flowers; without a sign, repentance brings no benefit
reciting the precepts once
twenty monks performing the procedure
quiz.why: "If one is repenting the ten major precepts, a favorable sign must be seen before the offense can be said to be extinguished — the Buddha coming to rub the crown of one's head, or seeing light, flowers, and other auspicious signs ... if no sign is seen, then even repentance brings no benefit."

quiz.q: Which correctly gives the four kinds of signs?
options: heat, coolness, lightness, heaviness
in dreams; a voice from space or unusual signs while walking; seeing signs of good, evil, keeping or breaking precepts while sitting; the mind of the path opening through inner realization
hell, snakes, the white curl, lotus
seeing Buddha, Dharma, Saṅgha, precepts
quiz.why: "First, seeing a sign in a dream; second, hearing a voice from empty space while walking the path, or seeing an extraordinary sign ...; third, beholding, while sitting, a sign of good, of evil, of having broken the precepts, or of having upheld them; fourth, taking as a sign the opening up of the mind of the path through various inwardly realized dharma-gates." Hell, snakes, and the white curl are objects of sign-contemplation from the Āgamas.

quiz.q: Māra can also produce such signs. How does the text say they are to be distinguished?
options: compare with the written descriptions
no need to distinguish; any sign means extinction
hard to tell; only a good teacher recognizes them, face to face, not through writing — so one must draw near a good spiritual friend
good signs are always the Buddha, bad ones always Māra
quiz.why: "The deviant and the correct are hard to distinguish ... only a good teacher can properly recognize it — this is a matter that must be settled face to face, and cannot be conveyed through writing alone. This is why a practitioner, when first taking up repentance, must draw near to a good spiritual friend." It warns that chasing the written description invites demonic interference.

quiz.q: What does the text say "contemplation of signs" really means?
options: simply apply the mind to the path; when effort bears fruit a sign appears and is used to judge — not dwelling on signs while practicing
reading people's faces
visualizing the Buddha's marks
fixing the mind on seeing an auspicious sign
quiz.why: "What is meant by 'contemplation of signs' is only this: applying the mind to walking the path, and, once this effort bears fruit, a sign appears of itself — one then takes this sign as a basis for judgment ... It does not mean that, while walking the path, the mind should dwell on the matter of a sign and give rise to grasping after it."

quiz.q: Why is sign-contemplation repentance explained mostly in terms of cultivating concentration?
options: because the four dhyānas must first be attained
because concentration matters more than precepts
because Māra cannot enter concentration
because all of it is carried out within a concentrated mind
quiz.why: "All of this is carried out within a concentrated mind, and so sign-contemplation repentance is, for the most part, explained in terms of the cultivation of concentration." This is why it supports concentration among the three methods.

quiz.q: In the Samantabhadra Contemplation Sūtra verse, "every offense is like frost or dew" — what follows?
options: which a great rain can settle
like a lamp in the wind
the morning dew vanishes at once
which the sun of wisdom can dissolve away
quiz.why: "Every offense is like frost or dew, which the sun of wisdom can dissolve away; / Hence, with a mind of utmost sincerity, repent at the very root of the six faculties of feeling."

quiz.q: From what, according to the text, do measureless grave offenses arise?
options: from external objects
all from a single thought-moment of unenlightened mind
from past karma
from Māra
quiz.why: "From these three poisons, every measureless and boundless grave offense is committed at length — all of it arising from a single thought-moment of unenlightened mind." Hence the practice turns back to ask where this mind arises.

quiz.q: In turning back on the mind, why can it not be found if it is said to be in the present?
options: because the present is outside the body
because the present has already ceased
because the present has not yet arrived
within the present not a moment remains still, and within what never remains, mind cannot be found
quiz.why: "If it is in the present, then within the present itself, not a single moment remains still — and within a mark that never remains still, mind cannot be found." "Already ceased" describes the past and "not yet arrived" the future.

quiz.q: To whom did Vimalakīrti say, "That offense is, of itself, without any offense — do not increase its fault"?
options: Upāli
Śāriputra
Ānanda
Subhūti
quiz.why: "Hence Vimalakīrti said to Upāli: 'That offense is, of itself, without any offense at all — do not increase its fault.'"

quiz.q: How does the text rank repentance through the contemplation of no-arising?
options: the same as sign-contemplation
it is the great repentance, most honored and sublime; every Mahāyāna sūtra on repentance takes it as the core
only for beginners
merely provisional, inferior to formal procedure
quiz.why: "Hence it is known that the deep contemplation of no-arising is called great repentance — the most honored, the most sublime of every form of repentance. In every Mahāyāna sūtra that explains the method of repentance, this contemplation is taken as the essential core."

quiz.q: In repentance by no-arising, besides signs appearing of themselves, what does the text say is itself the mark of extinction?
options: reciting precepts a thousand times
the saṅgha declaring it
dreaming of a buddha image
the contemplating mind coming into accord with principle is itself the mark, needing nothing further
quiz.why: "If a practitioner's contemplating mind comes into accord with principle itself, this is precisely the mark of the offense's extinguishing, with no further confirmation needed elsewhere."
